import numpy as np
from PyLTSpice import RawRead
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

raw = RawRead("../ngspice/NMOS.raw", dialect="ngspice")

par_names = raw.get_trace_names()

par_prefix = par_names[1].split('[')[0]

short_names = {}
for name in par_names:
    short_name = name.split('[', 1)[1].split(']', 1)[0] if '[' in name and ']' in name else name
    short_names[short_name] = name


var1 = raw.get_trace(short_names["id"]).get_wave()
var2 = raw.get_trace(short_names["vds"]).get_wave()
var3 = raw.get_trace(short_names["vgs"]).get_wave()
sweep = raw.get_trace(short_names["v(v-sweep)"]).get_wave()

v_sweep = np.array(list(dict.fromkeys(sweep)))

var1 = np.reshape(var1, (len(v_sweep), -1), order='F')
var2 = np.reshape(var2, (len(v_sweep), -1), order='F')
var3 = np.reshape(var3, (len(v_sweep), -1), order='F')
vgs = var3[0, :]


plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
plt.plot(var2, var1 * 1000)
plt.legend([f"VGS = {v:.2f} V" for v in vgs])

plt.xlabel("Vds (V)")
plt.ylabel("Id (mA)")
plt.grid(True)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Drain current \(I_D\) versus drain-source voltage \(V_{DS}\) for different \(V_{GS}\) values.






#target curve
target_vgs = 0.8
idx = np.argmin(np.abs(vgs - target_vgs))

title: Introduction to Analog Circuit Design
text:
Getting started
To start designing analog circuits, you need to understand the fundamentals of electronic circuits, including nodal and mesh analysis, Kirchhoff’s Current Law (KCL) and Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law (KVL), and, of course, transistors and other nonlinear devices.
Furthermore, you should be able to design and analyze basic circuit blocks using pen and paper. In other words, you should be able to understand and predict the behavior and functionality of basic circuit blocks before simulating them.
After designing a circuit, its functionality is verified through simulation, and modifications are made as necessary to achieve the desired performance. Therefore, we need a circuit simulator. Two popular simulators for analog IC design are Synopsys HSPICE and Cadence Spectre. Unfortunately, both of these tools require a paid license.
Fortunately, there are several free circuit simulators available for analog circuit design. Ngspice and LTspice are two well-known free SPICE circuit simulators. With LTspice, schematic capture and waveform viewing are integrated into the simulator. Ngspice, on the other hand, is primarily a SPICE-based simulator whose input is a circuit netlist and whose output consists of simulation data. Therefore, to work with schematics, you need a schematic capture tool, and to view simulation waveforms, you need a waveform viewer. In this course, we use Ngspice as the circuit simulator.
For schematic capture, there is a free and open-source tool called Xschem. Since Xschem supports hierarchical schematics, it is well suited for designing large and complex circuits. It is also supported by several open-source PDKs. Furthermore, Xschem provides an integrated waveform viewer, while also supporting external waveform viewers.
It is recommended to install Linux, as all of the essential tools run smoothly on Linux-based systems. Linux distributions are free, and if you are using Windows, you can easily set up a Linux environment through WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux). For example, I am using Ubuntu on WSL.
Below are the main tools used in a typical analog IC design flow:

Schematic Capture:
xschem — https://xschem.sourceforge.io/stefan/index.html
Circuit Simulation:
ngspice — https://ngspice.sourceforge.io
Layout Editor:
Magic VLSI — http://opencircuitdesign.com/magic/index.html
Open PDK:
SkyWater SKY130 — http://opencircuitdesign.com/open_pdks/index.html



Integrating Xschem with SKY130
There are clear instructions available for setting up xschem with the SKY130 PDK:
Documentation:
XSCHEM SKY130 INTEGRATION
A detailed video tutorial is also available, covering xschem, ngspice, and SKY130 PDK usage from scratch:
https://youtu.be/bYbkz8FXnsQ?si=K5OG5g5v23BnFscz

title: ACC–Designs R&D

Welcome to ACC Designs R&D!
This is my personal website about my work in analog custom circuit design. It primarily covers analog and mixed-signal IC design, including data converters, RF circuits and blocks, and various types of amplifiers.
It also covers selected topics in discrete circuit design, including basic analog circuit design, power electronics, and switch-mode power supplies (SMPS).

title: MOSFET Small-Signal Characteristics
text:
We will extract the small-signal characteristics of MOSFETs using freely available, open-source PDKs and CAD tools. The analysis is carried out using the SkyWater sky130 PDK, Xschem as the schematic capture tool, and Ngspice as the circuit simulator.
All tools (Xschem, Ngspice, and sky130 PDK) must be installed properly on a Linux system. In this overview, Ubuntu running under WSL is used. The installation procedure is discussed in a separate article.
The reader is assumed to have a basic understanding of MOSFET device physics and the fundamentals of MOSFET operation. Figure 1 illustrates the structure and symbols of NMOS and PMOS devices. In integrated-circuit design, a MOSFET has four terminals: gate (G), source (S), drain (D), and bulk (B). Modern CMOS technologies typically employ a p-type substrate; therefore, the bulk of all NMOS devices (except native devices) is tied to the substrate, i.e., GND or VSS. In contrast, PMOS devices are fabricated in isolated wells, allowing their bulks to be biased independently.

title: MOSFET Small-Signal Characteristics
text:
Saturation region:
Including channel length modulation, the mosfet current is given by:
\[
I_D=\frac{1}{2}\mu_nC_{ox}\frac{W}{L}\left(V_{GS}-V_{TH}\right)^2(1+\lambda\ V_{DS})
\tag{3}\]
The parameter \(\lambda\) is the channel-length modulation coefficient, which decreases with increasing channel length.
\[
\lambda\propto\frac{1}{L}
\tag{4}\]

title: MOSFET Small-Signal Characteristics
text:
Body effect:
Increasing the source-to-bulk voltage raises the threshold voltage:
\[
V_{TH}=V_{TH0}+\gamma\left(\sqrt{2\Phi_F+V_{SB}}-\sqrt{\left|2\Phi_F\right|}\right)
\tag{5}\]
\[
\gamma=\frac{\sqrt{2q\epsilon_{si}N_{sub}}}{C_{ox}}\approx0.3\ to\ 0.4\ \left(V^\frac{1}{2}\right)
\tag{6}\]
\[
V_{TH0}=\Phi_{MS}+2\Phi_F+\frac{Q_{dep}}{C_{ox}}=V_{TH}\ when\ V_{SB}=0
\tag{7}\]

title: MOSFET Small-Signal Characteristics
text:
Subthreshold (weak inversion):
When \(V_{GS} \approx V_{TH}\), the device enters weak inversion, and the drain current follows:
\[
I_D=I_0\exp{\frac{V_{GS}}{\xi V_T}}
\tag{8}\]
where \(I_0\) is proportional to \(W/L\), \(\xi > 1\), and \(V_T=kT/q\). The device is said to operate in weak inversion, as opposed to strong inversion.

title: MOSFET Small-Signal Characteristics
text:
Equations:
In triode region, a MOSFET behaves as a voltage-controlled resistor:
\[
R_{on}=\frac{1}{\mu_nC_{ox}\frac{W}{L}(V_{GS}-V_{TH})}
\tag{9}\]
In saturation, the transconductance is:
\[
g_m=\frac{\partial I_D}{\partial V_{GS}}
\tag{10}\]
Equivalent expressions include:
\[
g_m=\mu_nC_{ox}\frac{W}{L}(V_{GS}-V_{TH})
\tag{11}\]
\[
g_m=\sqrt{2\mu_nC_{ox}\frac{W}{L}I_D}
\tag{12}\]
\[
g_m=\frac{2I_D}{V_{GS}-V_{TH}}
\tag{13}\]
The output resistance due to channel-length modulation is:
\[
r_o=\frac{1}{g_{ds}}=\frac{\partial V_{DS}}{\partial I_D}=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{2}\mu_nC_{ox}\frac{W}{L}\left(V_{GS}-V_{TH}\right)^2\times\lambda}
\tag{14}\]
Given \(\lambda V_{DS} << 1\), we have
\[
r_o=\frac{1}{g_{ds}}=\frac{1+\lambda V_{DS}}{\lambda I_D}\approx\frac{1}{\lambda I_D}
\tag{15}\]
The body-effect transconductance is:
\[
g_{mb}=\frac{\partial I_D}{\partial V_{BS}}=gm\frac{\gamma}{2\sqrt{2\Phi_F+V_{SB}}}=\eta\ g_m
\tag{16}\]

title: MOSFET Small-Signal Characteristics
text:
Long-channel NMOS:
The circuit in Figure 3 is used to evaluate the small-signal, low frequency behavior of an NMOS device. Because capacitances are not considered in this section, DC-sweep analysis is employed.






Figure 3: Simple NMOS circuit used for DC-sweep analysis



Here, W/L = 100u/1.5u, number of gates (fingers) are 10, and the VGS sweep ranges from 0 to 1.8V. Figure 4 shows gm and gds of the NMOS versus VGS.












(a) \(g_m\) versus \(V_{GS}\)











(b) \(g_{ds}\) versus \(V_{GS}\)







Figure 4: Variation of \(g_m\) and \(g_{ds}\) versus \(V_{GS}\) for \(V_{DS}=1V\).




In this circuit, \(V_{TH} \approx 470mV\). As \(V_{GS}\) increases, both \(g_m\) and \(g_{ds}\) increase as expected. It’s interesting to see the gds – Id relationship as shown in Figure 5. The curve is nearly linear, and according to Equation 15, its slope corresponds to the channel-length modulation coefficient \(\lambda\).









Figure 5: Variation of \(g_{ds}\) versus Drain current \(I_d\) for \(V_{DS}=1.8V\).






The intrinsic small-signal gain of a MOSFET is defined as
\[
A_v = g_mr_o = \frac{g_m}{g_{ds}}
\tag{17}\]
The intrinsic gain of a long-channel NMOS transistor is shown in Figure 6. As can be seen, in saturation region, the gain peaks at approximately \(V_{GS}=0.56V\). This corresponds to an overdrive voltage of \(V_{ov}=V_{GS}-V_{TH}\approx 100mV\), at which the device achieves its maximum intrinsic gain. As \(V_{ov}\) increases further, the intrinsic gain decreases.









Figure 6: Intrinsic small-signal low-frequency gain of NMOS with W/L = 100u/1.5u.






For \(V_{ov}\) below roughly 80mV the device operates in the weak-inversion region. When \(V_{GS}<V_{TH}\), the transistor is off and the concept of intrinsic gain is no longer meaningful.

title: MOSFET Small-Signal Characteristics
text:
Short-channel NMOS:
For channel length below \(1\mu m\) (submicron), MOSFET behavior is significantly affected by short-channel and other higher-order effects. Figure 7 illustrates how these effects alter the small-signal parameters of a device with \(W/L = 10\mu m/ 0.15\mu m\). A detailed discussion of short-channel devices will be presented in a subsequent article.












(a) \(g_m\) versus \(V_{GS}\)











(b) \(g_{ds}\) versus \(V_{GS}\)













(c) \(g_m/g_{ds}\) versus \(V_{GS}\)











(d) \(g_{ds}\) versus \(I_d\)







Figure 7: Variation of small-signal parameters versus \(V_{GS}\) for short-channel NMOS where \(W=10 \mu m\) and \(L=0.15 \mu m\).

title: Design of a Simple OTA
text:
Amplifiers are among the most important blocks in analog IC design, as they are used in a wide range of analog and mixed-signal circuits, including active filters, integrators, sensor interfaces, sample-and-hold circuits, and data converters. When combined with an appropriate feedback network, an op-amp can perform mathematical operations, amplify small signals, and provide accurate signal conditioning. Its performance therefore has a significant impact on the overall performance of the systems in which it is used.
Several parameters must be considered when designing an op-amp. DC open-loop gain determines how accurately the amplifier can operate in a feedback configuration. Unity-gain bandwidth (UGBW) indicates the frequency at which the open-loop gain falls to unity, while phase margin provides an indication of closed-loop stability. Slew rate determines the maximum rate of change of the output voltage, and settling time specifies how quickly the output reaches and remains within a desired error range after an input transition. Other important parameters include power consumption, input-referred noise, input offset voltage, input common-mode range, output voltage swing, common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR), power-supply rejection ratio (PSRR), and silicon area. The relative importance of these parameters depends on the intended application and its requirements.
The general design flow for an analog circuit block is shown in Figure 1.






flowchart TD
A[Define design specifications] --> B[Select circuit topology]
B --> C[Perform hand calculations]
C --> D[Choose initial transistor dimensions and bias]
D --> E[Simulation]
E --> F[Modification]
F --> E 




Figure 1: Analog block design flow.





As a practical example, consider the design of a five-transistor operational transconductance amplifier (5T OTA) in a nominal 1.8 V CMOS process. This topology consists of an NMOS differential input pair, a PMOS current-mirror active load, and an NMOS tail-current source. It is an attractive starting point because of its simple structure, low transistor count, and relatively low power consumption. However, its single-stage architecture and limited output-voltage headroom constrain its gain, output swing, and driving capability. The target specifications for an illustrative design could be:

Supply voltage: 1.8 V
Load capacitance: 1 pF
DC gain: at least 40 dB
Unity-gain bandwidth: at least 100 MHz
Power consumption: < 200 \(\mu W\)

The first step is to select the CMOS process and its PDK. The PDK provides the transistor models, design rules, and other technology-specific information required for realistic circuit design.
Important parameters include transistor threshold voltages, current characteristics, output resistance, parasitic capacitances, and available channel lengths. These parameters influence the transistor dimensions, bias conditions, achievable gain, and bandwidth.
In a preliminary educational design, simplified MOSFET equations can be used to estimate the operating point and initial dimensions. However, these equations are based on approximations and cannot fully represent the behavior of actual CMOS transistors. The final transistor sizing must therefore be refined using the selected PDK models.
This article uses the open-source SkyWater SKY130 PDK because Ngspice device models are available, and Xschem can be used for schematic capture and simulation. Device models and parameters for the SKY130 PDK are available on the SKY130 Device Details page.

Topology
Once the specifications and technology are known, an appropriate amplifier topology can be selected.
The 5T OTA is a useful example because it consists of only five transistors: an NMOS differential input pair, a PMOS current-mirror active load, and an NMOS tail-current source, as shown in Figure 2. Its small transistor count makes the circuit suitable for illustrating fundamental analog IC design principles.






Figure 2: A simple 5T OTA schematic



Note that the device sizes in Figure 2 have not yet been determined; the figure shows only the topology. According to the SKY130 PDK documentation, the threshold voltage of MOS devices depends on W and L for both typical and LVT types. Thus, after designing the circuit and obtaining rough estimates of the device sizes, we can determine the threshold voltages and estimate the operating points. This design uses LVT devices.


Hand calculation
The next step is to translate the specifications into electrical requirements.
For example, the unity-gain bandwidth determines the approximate minimum transconductance required of the input transistors.
\[
2\pi f_u=\frac{g_{mN}}{C_L}
\tag{1}\]
where \(g_{mN}\) is the transconductance of the NMOS differential pair. The actual load capacitance is the sum of the load capacitor and the drain capacitances of M2 and M3, \(C_L + C_{d2} + C_{d3}\). Since the transistor sizes are still unknown, assume a load capacitance that is 10% higher than the specified value, or 1.1 pF. The minimum \(g_m\) is then
\[
g_{mN} \approx 2\pi f_uC_{L\mathrm{total}}\approx 700\mu \mho
\tag{2}\]
The other constraint is the amplifier’s DC gain, which must be greater than 40 dB, or 100. The intrinsic gain of the input differential pair must therefore be greater than 100. To meet this requirement, we need to choose appropriate sizes for the NMOS differential pair. In the SKY130 process, the minimum channel length is 0.15 um. At this minimum channel length, the maximum achievable intrinsic gain is about 15, as shown in Figure 3 (a). According to the square-law MOSFET model:
\[
g_m=\frac{2I_d}{V_{ov}},\quad
\frac{1}{g_{ds}}\approx \frac{1}{\lambda I_d}\implies
\frac{g_m}{g_{ds}}\approx \frac{2}{\lambda V_{ov}}
\tag{3}\]
This shows that, for a given \(V_{ov}\), a MOSFET’s intrinsic gain depends on \(\lambda\) and, consequently, on \(L\), while being almost independent of \(W\). Increasing \(L\) decreases \(\lambda\) and therefore increases intrinsic gain. Figure 3 (b) shows the intrinsic gain for \(L=1.5\mu m\). The maximum intrinsic gain is about 110, so we begin the design with \(L=1.5\mu m\).











(a) \(W/L=10\mu /0.15\mu\)











(b) \(W/L=100\mu /1.5\mu\)







Figure 3: NMOS intrinsic gain \(g_m/g_{ds}\) and \(g_m\) versus overdrive voltage \(V_{ov}\).



According to the square-law MOSFET model, \(g_m=2I_d/V_{ov}\). In submicron technologies, the coefficient is roughly 1.2 to 1.5. We can calculate the overdrive voltage of the input differential pair to achieve the required \(g_m\) shown in Equation 2. Given a maximum power consumption of 200 uW and a supply voltage of 1.8 V, let us choose a tail current of 100 uA, corresponding to \(I_d=50\mu A\). This determines the overdrive voltage \(V_{ov}\).
\[
V_{ov}\approx\frac{1.5}{g_{mN}/I_d}\approx100mV
\tag{4}\]
Note that an overdrive voltage below approximately 80 mV may push the MOSFET into the subthreshold region, where the device’s gain bandwidth drops significantly.
The OTA gain must be at least 40 dB, or 100.
\[
Gain=\frac{g_{mN}}{g_{ds2}+g_{ds3}}
\tag{5}\]
According to Figure 3 (b), \(g_{mN}/g_{ds2}\approx110\). To achieve a gain of 100, \(g_{ds3}\) must be roughly \(g_{ds2}/10\), which is quite small. Achieving this requires the PMOS active-load devices M3 and M4 to have very large widths and lengths, resulting in very large gate capacitances. This moves the active load pole and zero to lower frequencies, which cannot be ignored. Therefore, we must consider the effect of the active load on the OTA’s frequency response. The active load introduces a pole and a zero in the OTA’s frequency response, which can be approximated as follows:
\[
\omega_{p2}\approx\frac{g_{mP}}{C_{g3}+C_{g4}},\quad
\omega_{z1}\approx2\omega_{p2}  
\tag{6}\]
where \(C_{g3}\) and \(C_{g4}\) are the gate capacitances of M3 and M4, respectively. The zero is located at approximately twice the frequency of the pole. If the P2 pole is in the vicinity of the gain-bandwidth product, it will degrade the unity-gain bandwidth. We will see the effect of the active load on the OTA’s frequency response in the simulation section.
According to Figure 3 (b), for Vov=100mV, the gm is 1m for W/L=100/1.5. Therefore, we can choose W/L=40/1.5 for the input differential pair to achieve gm=700u. The tail current source can be designed with W/L=100/1.5 to achieve a current of 100uA. The PMOS active load can be designed with W/L=10/1.5. The OTA schematic, including the transistor sizes and operating points, is shown below.






Figure 4: Schematic of the OTA, transistor sizes and operating points



The branch currents of the OTA are 50 uA, and the overdrive voltages of the input differential pair are roughly 100 mV. The active-load PMOS transistors have overdrive voltages of 440 mV, which are much higher than those of the input pair. This is expected because the active load’s W/L ratio is set to 10/1.5 so that its pole is at a higher frequency than the unity-gain bandwidth.


Simulation
After hand calculations, sizing, and biasing, the next step is to simulate the circuit to verify its performance. The OTA was simulated using Ngspice with the SKY130 PDK models. The simulation results for the frequency response are shown below.






Figure 5: Frequency Response



The unity-gain bandwidth is approximately 100 MHz. The DC gain is about 38 dB, or 80, which is slightly below the target of 40 dB. The phase margin is about 71 degrees, which indicates good stability. The power consumption is about 180 uW, which is below the target of 200 uW.
